Clinical Reference

Pyelonephritis & Complicated UTI

On this page
Acute pyelonephritis is infection of the renal parenchyma and collecting system — fever + flank/CVA tenderness + pyuria/bacteriuria — and it becomes a “complicated” UTI whenever a host factor (male sex, pregnancy, catheter, obstruction/stone, diabetes, immunocompromise, transplant) raises the risk that antibiotics alone will fail. The obstructed, infected kidney is a surgical emergency.
E. coli in 75–95% Cipro 500 mg BID ×7 d (FQ resistance ≤10%) No improvement by 48–72 h → image (CT) ESBL bacteremia → carbapenem, not pip-tazo (MERINO) Obstructed + infected = emergent decompression Urosepsis: NE first, MAP ≥65, abx ≤1 h
Shared

Pathophysiology & classification

🧬

Mechanism — the story

Nearly all pyelonephritis is an ascending infection. Fecal/periurethral flora — overwhelmingly uropathogenic E. coli (UPEC) — colonize the urethra, climb into the bladder (cystitis), then ascend the ureter to the renal pelvis and parenchyma. Hematogenous seeding (e.g., S. aureus, Candida) is uncommon and hints at a distant source.

UPEC succeeds because of virulence factors: P-fimbriae / pili & adhesins latch onto uroepithelial glycolipid receptors, letting the organism resist urine washout and invade tissue — P-fimbriated strains disproportionately cause pyelonephritis and bacteremia. Urease-producers (Proteus, some Klebsiella) split urea into ammonia, alkalinizing urine and precipitating struvite (magnesium-ammonium-phosphate) “infection” stones that harbor bacteria and obstruct — a self-perpetuating loop. Toxins (hemolysin, CNF-1), siderophores, and the K-antigen capsule round out the arsenal.

Host defenses — the flushing of micturition, low pH / high osmolality, Tamm–Horsfall protein that traps fimbriated bacteria, urothelial antimicrobial peptides, and secretory IgA — normally win. Obstruction, stasis, or a foreign body tips the balance: stagnant urine is culture medium; obstruction raises intrapelvic pressure and drives pyelovenous/pyelolymphatic backflow → bacteremia; catheters and stones offer an abiotic surface for biofilm, a polysaccharide matrix that shields organisms from both antibiotics and immune cells and cannot be sterilized without removing the device. Parenchymal invasion unleashes a cytokine surge (IL-1, IL-6, TNF) → fever, bacteremia (~10–30% of hospitalized cases) → sepsis. In diabetics, tissue glucose plus gas-forming fermenters produce emphysematous pyelonephritis (EPN).

the urinary tract is a river system. The current (urine flow) normally sweeps debris downstream. A stone or catheter is a logjam: water pools, silt (bacteria) settles, and a slimy film (biofilm) coats the logs. No amount of chlorine (antibiotic) poured upstream clears a jam you don’t physically remove — which is why source control beats any drug in obstructed or abscessed disease.
Ascending route: colonization → cystitis → ureteral ascent → pyelonephritis → urosepsis. Any host factor (stone, catheter, obstruction) diverts the course into complicated disease where source control is decisive.
Acute left pyelonephritis — contrast CT shows wedge-shaped areas of reduced perfusion (striated nephrogram).
Hellerhoff, “Akute Pyelonephritis links mit Minderperfusion der linken Niere 52M - CT - 001.jpg”, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
Renal parenchymal inflammation — CD68 immunostain highlights sheets of lipid-laden macrophages in xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis, a chronic variant of unresolved infection.
Nephron, “Xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis cd68.jpg”, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
every antibiotic used here interrupts one specific bacterial machine. Beta-lactams and fosfomycin attack the cell wall; aminoglycosides jam the ribosome; fluoroquinolones snap the DNA-unwinding enzymes; TMP-SMX starves the bug of folate; nitrofurantoin is a shotgun that only reaches urine. Knowing the target explains why nitrofurantoin/fosfomycin can’t treat kidney tissue and why source control is non-negotiable when biofilm blocks drug access.
Drug classMolecular targetEffect & why it matters here
Beta-lactams
penicillins, cephalosporins, carbapenems, aztreonam		Penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs)Block peptidoglycan cross-linking → bactericidal wall lysis. Backbone of inpatient therapy; carbapenems for ESBL.
FluoroquinolonesDNA gyrase (topo II) + topoisomerase IVBlock DNA supercoiling/replication → bactericidal. Achieve high renal tissue + urine levels → ideal for pyelonephritis (resistance permitting).
Aminoglycosides30S ribosomal subunitCause mistranslation → concentration-dependent kill + synergy. Potent for Gram-negatives; nephro/ototoxic.
TMP-SMXDihydropteroate synthase + dihydrofolate reductaseSequential blockade of folate synthesis → bactericidal. Only if isolate susceptible.
FosfomycinMurA (enolpyruvyl transferase)Blocks the first committed step of wall synthesis. Urine-concentrating → cystitis only, not pyelonephritis.
NitrofurantoinMultiple enzymes/DNA (via nitroreductase)Broad, nonspecific damage but concentrates in urine only — no renal tissue levels → never for pyelonephritis; contraindicated CrCl <30.
Antibiotic target map — each class disables one bacterial machine. Nitrofurantoin/fosfomycin reach only urine (cystitis), so the upper tract needs a tissue-penetrating agent (fluoroquinolone, beta-lactam, aminoglycoside).
🗂️

Definitions & classification

IDSA 2010/2025 · EAU 2024
TermDefinition
Uncomplicated UTICystitis or pyelonephritis in a non-pregnant, premenopausal woman with a structurally/functionally normal tract and no relevant comorbidity.
Complicated UTI (cUTI)UTI + a factor raising failure risk. IDSA 2025 pragmatically defines cUTI as pyelonephritis, or UTI with systemic signs (fever, chills, hemodynamic instability), or UTI with urologic abnormality/instrumentation.
Acute pyelonephritisInfection of renal parenchyma + collecting system: flank pain/CVA tenderness + fever ± lower-tract symptoms + pyuria/bacteriuria.
Emphysematous pyelonephritis (EPN)Necrotizing gas-forming parenchymal infection; ~85% diabetic; graded by Huang–Tseng CT class 1–4.
Renal / perinephric abscessWalled-off pus in parenchyma or perinephric space; suspect when fever persists >72 h despite adequate antibiotics.
PyonephrosisPus within an obstructed collecting system — urologic emergency requiring immediate decompression.
UrosepsisSepsis with a urinary source; obstructive pyelonephritis can progress rapidly to septic shock.
CAUTIUTI signs/symptoms + culture ≥10³ CFU/mL in a catheterized (or ≤48 h post-removal) patient with no other source.
Asymptomatic bacteriuria (ASB)≥10⁵ CFU/mL (2 voided specimens in women; 1 in men; 1 catheterized) with no attributable symptoms — usually should NOT be treated.
What makes a UTI “complicated”? Male sex · pregnancy · indwelling/intermittent catheter or recent instrumentation · obstruction (stones, tumor, stricture, BPH) · immunocompromise · poorly controlled diabetes · renal transplant · neurogenic bladder · CKD · anatomic anomaly. EAU 2024 stresses separating uncomplicated from obstructive pyelonephritis early — the latter can become urosepsis fast.
Rising community ESBL E. coli (2024–25) has eroded empiric fluoroquinolone and 3rd-gen cephalosporin reliability, pushing carbapenem-sparing strategies and newer agents (ceftazidime-avibactam, meropenem-vaborbactam, imipenem-relebactam, cefiderocol) for MDR/CRE.

Dr Graham Beards, “Escherichia coli Gram Stain.jpg”, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
Struvite “staghorn” calculus — formed by urease-splitting organisms; a nidus and obstruction driving complicated, relapsing infection.
Nevit Dilmen (talk), “Staghorn Kidney Stone 08779.jpg”, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
When to suspect resistance (ESBL/AmpC/CRE): antibiotic exposure in the prior 1–3 months (strongest risk), prior hospitalization or ESBL history, travel to high-prevalence regions, long-term care residence, indwelling devices, or recurrent UTI on prophylaxis. The IDSA 2010 rule: empiric oral fluoroquinolone only where local uropathogen FQ resistance is ≤10%; avoid empiric TMP-SMX where local E. coli resistance exceeds ~20%.

Presentation — frequency & why it happens

Frequency color key: >70% · 40–70% · 15–40% · <15%

FeatureFrequencyWhy it happens
Flank / back pain~85–90%Renal capsular stretch + parenchymal inflammation
CVA tenderness~85%Direct renal/perinephric irritation on percussion
Fever ≥38 °C / rigors~75–90%Pyrogenic cytokines (IL-1, IL-6, TNF) from tissue invasion / bacteremia
Chills / rigors~70%Bacteremic showers triggering thermoregulatory response
Dysuria / frequency / urgency~40–70%Concurrent lower-tract (bladder) involvement
Nausea / vomiting~40–60%Visceral reflex + systemic inflammation (also limits oral therapy)
Gross hematuria~10–30%Mucosal/urothelial inflammation
CystitisPyelonephritis
Dysuria, frequency, urgency, suprapubic painAll of that plus fever, flank pain/CVA tenderness
No fever, no flank pain, no systemic toxicityRigors, nausea/vomiting, leukocytosis, possible bacteremia
Empiric therapy without culture acceptableAlways culture urine (± blood) before treating
Atypical presentations: the elderly may show only delirium, falls, or functional decline (but confusion + positive UA without urinary symptoms is usually ASB — look elsewhere); diabetics risk EPN, papillary necrosis, abscess, and may present in DKA/HHS; catheterized / neurogenic-bladder patients often lack dysuria and present with fever or new sepsis; immunocompromised patients have muted signs — image early and cover broadly.
🩺 Clinic — outpatient diagnosis, treatment & prevention
Assess

When to suspect & who can go home

🔍

Outpatient presentation & eligibility

Suspect pyelonephritis in anyone with fever + flank/CVA-angle tenderness, with or without lower-tract symptoms (dysuria, frequency), and pyuria on urinalysis. Cystitis alone has no fever, flank pain, or systemic toxicity.

Who can be managed as an outpatient (IDSA 2010): non-pregnant adult, hemodynamically stable, able to tolerate oral fluids and medications, adequate pain control, no suspicion of obstruction or abscess, no severe comorbidity, and reliable follow-up.

Outpatient-eligibility check — tap every factor present

Any single flag argues for admission rather than outpatient oral therapy.

Cannot tolerate PO / persistent vomiting admit
Hemodynamic instability / sepsis (SBP<100, HR>100, ↑lactate) admit
Pregnancy admit
Suspected obstruction / stone / abscess / EPN admit
Uncontrolled pain admit
Significant immunocompromise / transplant admit
Failed outpatient therapy (no improvement 48–72 h) admit
Unreliable follow-up / social barrier admit
0
No admission flags selected — outpatient oral therapy is reasonable if the workup is reassuring.
Workup

What to order & when

🧪

Labs & imaging

Urinalysis w/ microAll suspected cases. Pyuria (WBC/hpf, leukocyte esterase), nitrites (Enterobacterales), bacteriuria, ± WBC casts (specific for renal origin). Absence of pyuria makes UTI unlikely.Initial
Urine culture + sensitivitiesAlways in pyelonephritis (unlike cystitis) — pre-treatment, to confirm organism and tailor therapy at 48–72 h.Initial
Blood cultures ×2If admitted, toxic, or diagnostic uncertainty. Not routine for well outpatients.If toxic
BMP ± CBC, glucose/A1cIf dehydrated, comorbid, or diabetic; assesses renal function for drug dosing.Selective
CT abd/pelvis + IV contrastPreferred imaging when: no improvement at 48–72 h, suspected obstruction/stone, abscess or EPN, complicated host, or urosepsis. Shows striated nephrogram, abscess, gas, hydronephrosis.If indicated
Renal ultrasoundFirst-line when contrast/radiation should be avoided — especially pregnancy; screens for obstruction/hydronephrosis.Pregnancy
Pyuria — sheets of leukocytes (pus cells) on urine microscopy support active infection.
Ajay Kumar Chaurasiya, “Pus cells (dead leukocytes) in urine microscopy.jpg”, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
WBC cast — cylindrical mold of leukocytes from a renal tubule; when present, it localizes infection/inflammation to the kidney.
Ajay Kumar Chaurasiya, “WBC cast in urine.jpg”, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
Renal ultrasound in acute pyelonephritis — first-line imaging in pregnancy to exclude obstruction.
Kristoffer Lindskov Hansen, Michael Bachmann Nielsen and Caroline Ewertsen, “Ultrasonography of acute pyelonephritis.jpg”, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
Routine imaging is not needed for uncomplicated pyelonephritis that is responding. The trigger to image is failure to improve by 48–72 h or any suspicion of a drainable/obstructive problem.

Interpreting the labs — why each value moves

LabDirectionMechanism & confounders (what falsely raises/lowers it)
Leukocyte esterase (UA)PositiveEsterase from urinary neutrophils → marks pyuria. False-neg: dilute urine, early infection, high glucose/protein. False-pos: vaginal contamination.
Nitrites (UA)PositiveEnterobacterales reduce dietary nitrate → nitrite; specific but insensitive. False-neg: short bladder dwell time, non-nitrate-reducers (Enterococcus, Staph, Pseudomonas), low dietary nitrate.
Pyuria (WBC/hpf)↑Neutrophil influx into urine. Sterile pyuria: think stones, TB, interstitial nephritis, prior antibiotics, or contamination. Absence makes UTI unlikely.
WBC castsPresentLeukocytes molded in a tubule → localizes to the kidney (pyelonephritis, interstitial nephritis). Rarely seen but highly informative.
Serum WBC↑ (left shift)Cytokine-driven marrow release/demargination. Confounders: steroids, stress; falsely low in overwhelming sepsis or immunosuppression — leukopenia is a bad sign.
Creatinine↑Sepsis hypoperfusion, obstruction, or nephrotoxins → AKI. Confounders: baseline CKD, volume status; drives all antibiotic dosing.
Lactate↑Tissue hypoperfusion / anaerobic metabolism → sepsis-severity marker. Confounders: β-agonists, liver dysfunction, seizure, metformin can raise it independent of perfusion.
Procalcitonin / CRP↑Bacterial-inflammation markers; support systemic infection and can trend response. Confounders: renal failure, surgery, non-infectious inflammation.
Blood culturePositiveBacteremia (10–30% of hospitalized APN); confirms organism & severity. Confounder: skin-flora contamination (single bottle, CoNS).

Key imaging findings (CT abd/pelvis with contrast, unless noted)

FindingWhen it appearsWhat it changes
Striated nephrogram (wedge-shaped hypoperfusion)Classic sign of acute pyelonephritis on contrast CTConfirms parenchymal infection; no drainable target → continue antibiotics
Hydronephrosis / obstructing stoneUltrasound or CT; look first in the sick or non-responding patientObstructed + infected = emergent decompression (PCN/stent)
Parenchymal / perinephric gasEmphysematous pyelonephritis, usually diabeticHuang–Tseng grading; drainage-forward management ± nephrectomy
Rim-enhancing fluid collectionRenal/perinephric abscess; suspect if fever >72 h despite abxSize-driven: <3 cm abx, 3–5 cm drain, >5 cm drain±surgery
Perinephric fat strandingCommon, nonspecific inflammatory changeSupports diagnosis; not itself a drainage target
Focal nephronia / renal enlargementSevere focal pyelonephritis (pre-abscess)Longer course; re-image if not resolving

Best renal tissue + urine penetration; short courses.

fluoroquinolones inhibit DNA gyrase/topoisomerase IV and reach high concentrations in both urine and renal parenchyma — the two compartments that matter in pyelonephritis.

The 10% rule: if local uropathogen FQ resistance is >10% — or you are not using a fluoroquinolone — give an initial long-acting parenteral “kick-start” dose first: ceftriaxone 1 g IV/IM once, or a consolidated once-daily aminoglycoside (gentamicin ~5–7 mg/kg).

Monitor

Follow-up & recurrence prevention

📈

What to recheck, and when

Expect defervescence and symptomatic improvement within 48–72 h. If not improving: re-culture, obtain CT, reassess for obstruction/abscess/resistance, and admit. Routine test-of-cure culture is not recommended when symptoms resolve (except in pregnancy).

Recurrent-UTI prevention (AUA/CUA/SUFU 2019, amended)

StrategyDose / detailEvidenceNote
Continuous antibiotic prophylaxisNitrofurantoin 50–100 mg qHS · TMP-SMX 40/200 mg qHS · cephalexin 125–250 mg qHSReduces recurrence — offer after counselingLowest effective dose; resistance/side-effect trade-off
Post-coital prophylaxisSingle dose after intercourseIf temporally relatedSame agents
Vaginal (topical) estrogenPer productRecommended in peri-/post-menopausal rUTIRestores urothelial defenses
Cranberry / behavioral / hydration—May offer (low-quality evidence)Adjuncts only
Do not treat asymptomatic bacteriuria to prevent recurrence — it drives resistance and C. difficile without benefit.

GradeRecommendationPopulation

Treat ASB in only two settings (IDSA 2019): pregnancy and before a urologic procedure with expected mucosal trauma. Not in diabetics, elderly, catheters, or spinal-cord injury.
Escalate

When to refer / admit

🚑

Red flags → ED / admission

Persistent vomiting or inability to keep PO · hemodynamic instability / sepsis physiology · uncontrolled pain · pregnancy · suspected obstruction, abscess, or EPN · significant immunocompromise · no improvement after 48–72 h of appropriate outpatient therapy. Any of these → send to the ED / admit.
🛏️ Wards — acute inpatient management
Admit

Who to admit

📋

Admission criteria

Admit pyelonephritis for any of:

  • Inability to tolerate PO (vomiting) or maintain hydration
  • Hemodynamic instability / sepsis physiology
  • Pregnancy with pyelonephritis (admit essentially all)
  • Suspected or confirmed obstruction, abscess, or EPN
  • Failed outpatient therapy (no improvement at 48–72 h)
  • Uncontrolled pain
  • Significant comorbidity / immunocompromise / transplant
  • Concern for nonadherence or poor follow-up
The single most important early branch point: is the infected kidney obstructed? Obstructive pyelonephritis is a different disease — it needs emergent decompression, not just antibiotics.

De-escalation & IV→PO switch: switch to a susceptibility-guided oral agent when afebrile ~48 h, hemodynamically stable, tolerating PO, and clinically improving. Total duration: fluoroquinolone 7 d (IDSA 2010; IDSA 2025: 5–7 d); non-fluoroquinolone 7 d; 7 d even for bacteremic cUTI (IDSA 2025); β-lactam course 10–14 d; men / suspected prostatitis 10–14 d; abscess/EPN/obstruction → individualized, source-control-driven.
Interactions

Comorbidities & drugs to avoid

🔗

How comorbidity changes course & management

ComorbidityHow it changes the diseaseDrug: avoid / prefer
DiabetesEPN, papillary necrosis, abscess; worse outcomes; may present in DKA/HHSAggressive glucose + sepsis control; image early
PregnancyAdmit for pyelonephritis; risk of preterm birth; treat ASB (screen — USPSTF B)Avoid: fluoroquinolones, TMP (1st trimester), sulfonamides near term (kernicterus), nitrofurantoin near term & G6PD, tetracyclines. Prefer: β-lactams (ampicillin, cephalexin, ceftriaxone)
CKD / renal impairmentReduced drug clearance; nephrotoxin riskNitrofurantoin contraindicated CrCl <30 (and useless anyway); renally dose β-lactams/carbapenems/FQ; aminoglycoside by level
Renal transplantImmunosuppressed; graft at risk; atypical organismsBroad early coverage; watch FQ/azole–calcineurin-inhibitor interactions; low imaging threshold
Stones / obstructionNidus + obstruction → complicated/urosepsis; struvite from urease organismsSource control (decompression/stone removal) mandatory
Indwelling catheter (CAUTI)Biofilm; polymicrobial; device can't be sterilizedReplace/remove catheter if in >2 weeks; don’t treat ASB; treat 7 d (up to 10–14 if delayed response)
Immunocompromise / neutropeniaMuted signs; rapid progression; resistant/fungalBroad empiric; add antifungal if candiduria + risk
ElderlyAtypical (delirium, falls); ASB common — don’t overtreatRenal dosing; FQ CNS/tendon caution; avoid treating ASB
Drugs to avoid / use with caution: Fluoroquinolones carry FDA boxed warnings — disabling tendon rupture, peripheral neuropathy, CNS/psychiatric effects, QT prolongation, aortic aneurysm/dissection (2018), and hypoglycemia/mental-health effects (2018); reserve for uncomplicated UTI only when no alternative. Nitrofurantoin — never for pyelonephritis; avoid CrCl <30, near term, and in G6PD deficiency. Aminoglycosides — nephro/ototoxic; monitor levels and avoid nephrotoxin stacking (IV contrast, vancomycin, NSAIDs, ACEi/ARB during AKI).
Monitor

Daily management

📈

What to trend each day

  • Temperature curve — expect defervescence by 48–72 h
  • Hemodynamics / MAP, HR — resolving tachycardia is a good sign
  • Urine output and renal function / electrolytes
  • WBC and lactate clearance
  • Culture & susceptibility results — de-escalate as soon as available
  • Reassess for obstruction/abscess (image) if not improving by 48–72 h
Escalate

When to call ICU

⬆️

Escalation triggers & sepsis scoring

Floor → ICU if: MAP <65 mmHg despite ~30 mL/kg crystalloid or any vasopressor requirement · lactate ≥4 mmol/L or failure to clear · respiratory failure (rising O₂ need, RR persistently ≥22–30, hypoxemia) · worsening organ dysfunction (rising creatinine, altered mentation, DIC) · obstructive urosepsis awaiting emergent decompression.

qSOFA (Sepsis-3) — bedside risk

1 point each; ≥2 flags higher risk of poor outcome → full assessment / escalate.

Respiratory rate ≥22/min +1
Systolic BP ≤100 mmHg +1
Altered mentation (GCS <15) +1
0
Low bedside risk.

SIRS criteria

≥2 of 4 = SIRS; with infection = clinical sepsis syndrome.

Temp >38 °C or <36 °C +1
Heart rate >90 bpm +1
Resp rate >20/min (or PaCO₂ <32) +1
WBC >12 or <4 ×10⁹/L (or >10% bands) +1
0
SIRS negative.

Full SOFA (6 organ systems) drives the Sepsis-3 definition — compute at MDCalc SOFA. Sepsis = suspected infection + acute SOFA rise ≥2; septic shock = vasopressors for MAP ≥65 + lactate >2 despite fluids.

Dispo

Discharge & disposition

🏠

Readiness + where they go

Discharge readiness: afebrile, hemodynamically stable, tolerating oral antibiotics, pain controlled, source controlled (or a definite plan in place), and reliable follow-up arranged. Not yet if: still febrile/tachycardic, borderline BP, undrained abscess/obstruction, persistent vomiting, or unresolved bacteremia without source control.

Home

Stable, tolerating PO abx, can complete the course independently.

Home health / OPAT

Needs continued IV (abscess, ESBL) → outpatient parenteral antibiotic therapy with nursing visits.

SNF

Deconditioned, needs 24 h skilled nursing / IV access, <3 h therapy/day.

Acute rehab (IRF)

Can tolerate ≥3 h therapy/day across ≥2 disciplines after prolonged illness.

LTAC

Prolonged complex care (e.g., vent weaning, long IV courses) >25 days.

Hospice / palliative

Recurrent urosepsis at end of life; comfort-focused goals.
🫀 ICU — urosepsis, septic shock & source control
Admit

ICU triggers & the 1-hour bundle

🚨

When it belongs in the unit

Triggers: septic shock (vasopressor need to keep MAP ≥65 + lactate >2 after resuscitation), respiratory failure, obstructive urosepsis needing emergent drainage, EPN, or multi-organ dysfunction.

Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021 — initiate within 1 hour of recognizing septic shock: (1) measure lactate (remeasure if >2); (2) blood cultures before antibiotics; (3) broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 h; (4) crystalloid 30 mL/kg for hypotension or lactate ≥4 (2021: weak rec — individualize with dynamic assessment); (5) vasopressors to MAP ≥65 if hypotensive during/after fluids.
Monitor

Monitoring & access

🩸

Lines, labs, targets

  • Arterial line for continuous BP/MAP once on vasopressors
  • Central venous access if escalating/multiple pressors
  • Serial lactate to guide resuscitation (target clearance)
  • Urine output (goal ≥0.5 mL/kg/h) + continuous telemetry
  • Dynamic fluid-responsiveness (passive leg raise, pulse-pressure variation) rather than fixed CVP targets
Source

Source control — the decisive move

🩹

Decompression & drainage

An obstructed, infected collecting system (pyonephrosis / obstructing stone) demands EMERGENT decompression — percutaneous nephrostomy (PCN) or retrograde ureteral stent — before definitive stone treatment. Antibiotics alone will not save an obstructed kidney; choice of PCN vs stent is driven by availability, coagulation status, and anatomy (broadly comparable early efficacy).
ProblemThresholdIntervention
Renal/perinephric abscess<3 cmIV antibiotics alone often sufficient
Renal/perinephric abscess3–5 cmPercutaneous drainage + antibiotics (~92% resolution)
Renal/perinephric abscess>5 cmDrainage (often multiple) ± surgery
Emphysematous PNParenchymal gas (Huang–Tseng class 2/3)Medical therapy + glycemic/sepsis control + percutaneous drainage; nephrectomy only for drainage failure/deterioration
Obstructing stone + infectionAnyEmergent PCN or ureteral stent; delayed definitive stone therapy
Broad empiric coverage in the ICU: antipseudomonal β-lactam or carbapenem (meropenem 1–2 g IV q8h) backbone; add vancomycin if MRSA/enterococcal/hardware concern; add an antifungal (echinocandin or fluconazole) if candidemia/candiduria with instrumentation. Cover ESBL/CRE per local epidemiology and prior cultures.
Support

Vasopressors

💉

Which drip, why, and the dose

Target MAP ≥65
AgentReceptors / mechanismDose rangeHemodynamic effectWhen to pick
NorepinephrinePotent α1 + modest β10.05–0.5+ mcg/kg/min↑SVR, mild ↑COFirst-line in septic shock
VasopressinV1 vascular (non-catecholamine)0.03 units/min (fixed; not titrated)↑SVR, catecholamine-sparingAdd-on when NE ~0.25–0.5 mcg/kg/min
Epinephrineβ1/β2 + α1~0.01–0.5 mcg/kg/min↑CO + ↑SVR2nd/3rd-line; low cardiac output
PhenylephrinePure α1~0.5–5 mcg/kg/min↑SVR (may reflex ↓HR)Niche — tachyarrhythmia limiting NE
DopamineDose-dependent D/β/αnot preferredvariableAvoid routinely; select bradycardic patients only
septic shock is vasodilatory — the problem is a collapsed systemic vascular resistance. Norepinephrine’s α1 agonism restores vascular tone (raising MAP) while its mild β1 activity supports cardiac output; vasopressin adds a second, non-adrenergic vasoconstrictor pathway (V1) to reach target while sparing catecholamine dose and its arrhythmia risk.
Airway

Respiratory support & vent

🌬️

If sepsis-induced hypoxemia / ARDS develops

Most urosepsis is managed without intubation. Escalate to invasive ventilation for sepsis-associated respiratory failure or ARDS (from the systemic inflammatory response); use lung-protective settings.

Downgrade

When to downgrade

⬇️

De-escalation to the floor

ICU → floor when: off vasopressors and hemodynamically stable for several hours · lactate normalized/clearing · improving mentation and renal function · adequate oxygenation off high support · source controlled (drain/stent in place, abscess drained) · antibiotics de-escalated to a targeted regimen. Consider LTAC for prolonged IV/complex needs; revisit goals of care in recurrent urosepsis at end of life.
